summary: In Greek mythology, according to Homer's Odyssey, Eurydice (Ancient Greek: Εὐρυδίκη, "wide justice"), eldest daughter of Clymenus, was the wife of Nestor of Pylos. Apollodorus instead names Anaxibia as Nestor's wife and mother of his children — a classic same-queen, different-name clash.
attribution: Adapted from Wikipedia, "Eurydice (daughter of Clymenus)" · CC BY-SA 4.0

sections.heading: Homer's queen of Pylos
paragraphs: In the Odyssey, when Nestor's household holds a hecatomb to Athena, the women raise the sacred cry — the daughters, the sons' wives, and "the revered wife of Nestor, Eurydice, eldest of the daughters of Clymenus" (Odyssey 3.450–452). Fair Polycaste, youngest daughter of Nestor, bathes Telemachus in the same episode; Homer names the queen but does not spell out each child's maternity in that passage.

Nestor's living sons in the Odyssey include Echephron, Stratichus, Aretus, Thrasymedes, and Peisistratus; Antilochus had fallen at Troy. Hyginus' Trojan catalogue makes Thrasymedes explicitly a son of Nestor by Eurydice.

sections.heading: Apollodorus' Anaxibia
paragraphs: According to Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 1.9.9), the wife of Nestor and mother of his children — daughters Pisidice and Polycaste, and sons Perseus, Stratichus, Aretus, Echephron, Peisistratus, Antilochus, and Thrasymedes — was Anaxibia, daughter of Cratieus. The atlas records this as a disputed queen-identity rather than merging the two names into one undisputed figure.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: This atlas entry (eurydice-nestor) is Nestor's Homeric queen, daughter of Clymenus. Distinct from Eurydice wife of Orpheus (eurydice-orpheus), Eurydice wife of Creon of Thebes (eurydice-thebes), and a Danaid Eurydice (eurydice-danaid).
